title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga is a game I'm quite torn on. While there are many aspects of the experience I absolutely adore, there is a large element to this game which I feel drags the experience down, making it not an immediate recommend I know it should be. To get to the best part of the game over with: presentation. The visuals are absolutely breathtaking and I found myself entranced playing through this game. Every character had personality oozing from their design alone and each boss you encounter feels lovingly thought of. [spoiler]I really felt this way about the Yellow and White Gods you see in the game. There is a sense of scale each of them have which does make you feel how daunting these 'Gods' are to our characters.[/spoiler] The visuals, alone, are not solely what carries this game. The music brought me into the world. Where many games I find enjoyable, but something I'm not going to think back on, Small Saga's soundtrack heightens the overall experience. The emotions are brought to another level when you play through, aiding to the story in more ways than you realize. From the lows to the highs, and the bosses through, the soundtrack assists in making a memorable presentation in the time you put in. The story is nothing amazing, but it's quite serviceable enough. The writing, overall, is enough to get you through. Yet I did find myself wanting more in. I would have loved more quests which allow you to learn more about the characters in the game. More people to interact with. I just found myself wanting more. The lore you do find in the books just feels a little clunky to me, making me just wish there was another manner to explore this world I'm shown. That said, the writing was enough to make me want to see more of this game. Now, the gameplay, which is where my experience takes a dip. It feels like the game focused on every other issue, yet the gameplay and everything surrounding it took a step back. Lacking is a word that immediately comes to mind, but even that might not properly do it justice. Despite the presentation and writing which all kept me coming in, the mechanics in the game was pushing me away. The game felt like it needed a vehicle to have their game, and made a passable RPG experience in order to do so. What is here was clearly given enough time to make it not completely arbitrary, yet not delved too deep into and allowing for a more fleshed out playthrough. For $20, this game is on the edge for me. Everything truly is incredible for this game, yet the game mechanics bring it down quite a bit for me. It takes what could easily have been a homerun and makes me more on the fence. Yet, if the game goes on sale at all, I would highly recommend picking this game up. Despite my feelings on the gameplay, Small Saga clearly had passion put behind it when it comes to presentation. And I think, if you can get past the mostly average mechanics, you do have a beautiful game awaiting you on the otherside.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga was pretty mediocre. There are some pretty cute moments where I enjoyed the characters and how they reacted to the events unfolding. However, the overall story operates at so much of a breakneck pace that it makes character development incredibly jarring; characters will flip motivation on a dime just to railroad the main plot. In the span of ~6 hours, you [spoiler] help a child run away from home, start a prison break which leads to overthrowing an authoritarian town and installing a new leader, start a revolution against the monarchy, overthrow a slaver, and help a person reconcile their past[/spoiler]. The game honestly tries to do too much too fast, which makes transitioning between main story beats turbulent. This results in characters not realistically offering pushback on others or having instantaneous changes of heart. Simultaneously, new ideas and information on people’s past are constantly introduced, but never meaningfully utilized or elaborated on. Many of the main story conflicts are resolved off screen and are only barely mentioned being resolved in a few sentences. A few characters are particularly loathsome with cringy dialogue in the form of forced memes. There are also several references to memes that were topical at the time. Constant attempts at humor are made but they mostly fall flat. The story takes up the vast majority of the game with some light amount of boss combat near the climax of each plot point. The combat is extremely vapid to the point it feels like a fantasy story masquerading as an RPG. There aren’t any meaningful decisions to make in terms of building character skills or gear. In fact, the game has several skills that increase damage to different types of enemies that either appear in only 2 combats or only in one chapter. I never felt in danger during combat and it boiled down to spamming damage abilities with no thought. It is very dissonant to be a meek rodent trying to rise up against larger creatures while combat is never dangerous. The final boss of the game was doing attacks that did 2 damage to me. There is a lack of polish that hampers the storytelling experience. Many important story moments had no music or ambient sound that made reading the dialogue emotionally hollow. Nearly every cutscene in the game used fades to black to hide actions being performed, items being placed, etc. There are also many incredibly long walkways between story areas that don’t serve any purpose to gameplay or storytelling. They don’t build atmosphere and just pad playtime as you meander through empty halls in dead silence. Overall, I found Small Saga to be entertaining enough to want to see the game through. The game was gifted to me and I think if I had spent the $15 myself, I would be more disappointed. For that reason, I can’t really recommend this game to others for its price. The plot is too hasty and needs to take more time so that many of the introduced threads are not hand waved away.

title: ELDEN RING
analysis_text: A short review of Elden Ring (Shadow of the Erdtree DLC included) Pros: - Simple controls and good playability. - Music and sounds are generally great. - Quite enjoyable single player campaign. - Graphics are good in most areas. Some are rather ugly or even disgusting, but this might be expected from a horror RPG. Cons: - Outdated combat system copied from earlier games without much revision. Every major flaw that existed in game mechanics over 17 years ago are still present in Elden Ring. - Game consists mostly of combat with very little other RPG elements. This might not be a bad thing if the combat system was better. - Worst co-op game of all time. Very little options and PVP cannot be disabled. - No real reason to play this more than once. The world is always the same, and you can do everything that's worth doing with just one character.

analysis_text: I have played Elden Ring for 73 Hours over the last, 3 years or so. I really like the game, but it simply isn't for me. I have restarted the game on a new character three times now, and am constantly failing at the games leveling system. I play through, wreck havoc on bosses, and more, but eventually, I hit the mid-late game area's and I'm ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Not because the enemies are tough, which they are, but because I'm kinda under leveled. Throughout the game, you are given hundreds of really, really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool weaponry. And during this entire process, it feels like you are expected to pick one, and stick with it for the entire game. That isn't really how I like to play RPG's. I love my Claymore sure, but I want to try out other weapons on bosses, different builds, constantly. And this game makes it very hard to do that. I always end up with incredibly evenly spread out stats, because I wanted to try out a certain weapon effectively, and it blisters my supposed build. Bosses begin to take upwards of 20-30 minutes to kill. It, becomes a slog. So I put down the game that year. And I pick it up 8 months later to continue this cycle. Every time I play again, it feels fresh, my build, though ♥♥♥♥♥♥, feels somewhat fresh again. And then it dulls, and I drop it again. At this point, I'm just going to mod it. I love this game, but its progression isn't for me.

analysis_text: To those who loved OneShot, this is another story-driven game. Of course, this game is much more tame compared to the puzzle aspect of OneShot. As the description suggests, you follow two scientists fulfilling a man's wish to go to the moon. You go through his old memories, and ones he's blocked off mysteriously. title: OneShot
analysis_text: Let me be clear I don't think that this is a bad game. If there was a neutral option I would have picked it, I just have a little bit more negative than positive. First the positives. I like the character designs. Everyone really sticks out and the different kinds of creatures make the world feel unique. I think that the concept of not only having to solve puzzles that have a point and click adventure style, but also having to do things on your computer is a nice concept and it had a few puzzles that I thought were really cool and had a lot of fun playing with. Niko is a very cute and fun protagonist and I definitely grew to really like him over the time i spent playing the game. My problems though are as follows. I think that the character writing is overall weak other than Niko. We don't get enough time with each characters or have conversations enough about them to really get an idea of who they are, and it's really disappointing. you always feel like the characters are just in the world that you are passing through and you only ever interact with them because you need them to solve a puzzle. It's a dang shame, because I really like the designs of each of the characters, I just wish there was more substance there. I wish that there were more dialogue options when interacting with Niko to give you more of a relationship with him. As I said previously, I really like him as a character, but I wanted more things to talk to him about and maybe have him remember things you told him before and have reactions to things in the world based on that. You have a few moments like that around the end, but you don't get to really interact with him in depth more than the main plot demands, and even then you only get two options that don't cover a lot of ground. The Solstice route, which could have been upping the anti by a lot in some really interesting ways as well as fleshing out the characters more, ended up being the weakest part of the game. The puzzles were either things you have already seen or were things that were done in a way more impressive manner in earlier playthroughs, leading to an underwhelming feeling when doing them. The characters get a little bit more dialogue but end up just treading over the same ground that they already did in the fist route rather than adding to the characters in any meaningful ways. some of which don't even get names until the end of the game. Some of the new characters are okay, but ultimately they just take away time we could be connecting further with the already established characters just to add more characters that we spend even less time with. The overall tension in the story felt force and predictable, and the ending felt cheap like it made everything that happened before meaningless. it was very disappointing. Overall it is not a bad game and has real potential and cool game mechanics, it just feels like it always falls short of the mark and leaves me wanting more.

Every character other than Niko does not have a fully-developed personality. Finding the solutions is VERY engaging. - I was invested in the world. It seemed like a living, breathing world. In the end, [spoiler]I chose Niko because I felt like there was literally no reason for me to choose the world that didn't make me try to care about it. Niko was the only character who was fully fleshed out.[/spoiler] - The music is pretty decent. It fit the vibe of every region, and no track felt out of place. [b]Given these points, I would recommend games like Undertale or OMORI to someone looking for a game with this kind of theme. If you're looking for a good puzzle game, though, this is definitely for you. The game succeeds as a puzzle game, but fails to deliver the compelling narrative and character development that I was looking for- and that I was constantly told about.[/b] SPOILERS: P.S. title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: [b]Ikenfell[/b] is a game that I really could not bring myself to enjoy. As a big fan of JRPGs and great pixel art, I was excited to see what this game had in store. 9 hours of slowly becoming more and more jaded later, I cannot get behind this game in any light. First of all, the sprite art is alright. Nothing insanely pretty, it’s obviously an RPGMaker game that takes a lot of inspiration from Earthbound and Undertale. I usually love the visuals in these games but in Ikenfell it was only so-so. The character sprites were peculiar to me, opting for 3 different styles, in exploration, in dialogue, and during combat. The most appealing version is during dialogue, where you can actually see the character’s faces, while during exploration they give a strangely large amount of pixel real estate to the character’s hair, only giving 3 tall pixels worth of a face. It makes the characters look very odd during top-down cutscenes and really disconnects me from the characters (because I cannot see their eyes). In addition, I found the combat to be an absolute slog. While I did find the idea somewhat interesting, and the lack of MP gave a lot more freedom to what spells you used, EVERY single fight is dragged on horrendously long. Even the most basic enemies take at least 3 or 4 turns from the player, complete with enemies moving AND attacking AND you having to block it. It turns what could be a 30 second encounter to 4 or 5 minutes, which in the long run becomes agonizingly long. Enemies become insane damage sponges and become entirely dependent on the timing of your attacks (which can be done automatically through settings). Also, the vocal tracks during the boss battles, while a novel idea, did not mesh at all with the gameplay, in fact it really took me out of the game. The story itself felt embarrassingly shallow for how much dialogue there is. I understand in a 10-15 hour game with lots of characters you can’t be expected to get huge development out of each of them, but every character felt so insanely cookie cutter that I couldn’t connect with a single one of them. Each character’s arc just flipped from one end of the other, the mean girl suddenly becomes nice, the shy girl gets brave, it’s just so tiring and I found myself caring less and less about the characters as the game progressed. The actual story of the game is even more unengaging but in the opposite way, plot threads get so quickly muddled and confusing that by the end of the game you’re unsure what is actually happening, somehow the characters talk so much but never about the thing you want to know more about. I respect the hell out of video-game creators, as they’ve made some of my favorite experiences I’ve ever consumed, and I think this is a great team with a lot of potential to make something truly special. But I don’t think this game respects the time of the consumer, it got to the point where I just started using the auto-victory for every boss near the end because it was becoming such a slog. I do think that if you really don’t mind a standard story and you auto-victory through some of the longer, more tedious bosses you could enjoy this game. But as it stands, Ikenfell, to me, is a dangerous combination of a monotonous battle system paired with fiercely rooted archetypal characters and a confusing story that they never bother to truly explain beyond “it’s magic!!”.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Ikenfell is one of literally thousands of 2D JRPG ripoffs infesting Steam, although at least this one was "genuinely" made instead of being asset flipped from the godawful RPG Maker construction kit. That doesn't mean, by a long shot, that this lazy, badly done console port is the kind of game any self respecting PC gamer would touch with a 10' pole. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard. A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result. There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings. There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. PC gamers will be insulted by the presence of console peasant children's toy controller prompts, despite this being on PC. Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for. Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies. Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for. These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers. The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game. Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone. These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game. Ikenfell has a truly insulting price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games (with 3D graphics instead of pixelcrap!), let alone the sheer number of free games available on Steam. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the questionable ethical nature of the developer and/or their associates (as outlined above), this is impossible to recommend.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Ikenfell is by far the queerest game I have ever played. I do appreciate the representation, but it can be a bit much. Not that it's a detriment, but as the story progressed it got a bit silly. However, the writing was decent, mostly, and it didn't come across as pandering... just a bit hamfisted at times. The gameplay itself was solid. The battle system was inspired by megaman battle network... but it does get repetitive. Around the halfway point of the game you get the best character. And it just makes all battles battles of attrition over difficult. The hidden bosses just really show it too. Not difficult, just gets tedious. But, that brings to mind a different strength of the game... accessibility options. One of which I had no problem enabling... "Instant win battles" for these long annoying fights. So overall, I'd say it's a pass and instead you can read any of your favorite gay star wars fanfiction.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: Great follow-up to To the Moon and another reminder that I really love these playable novel type games. What makes this one so fun is the mix of mystery and banter. I was always curious about what was really going on, what we were about to learn, and where the story was heading next. That kept me hooked the whole way through. At the same time, Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene make everything entertaining scene by scene, and Watts especially was a huge part of the fun for me with all his sarcasm, jokes, and random references. The low-friction interaction helps too, because the game stays focused on what it does best. The music and atmosphere were excellent! Now I’m really looking forward to Impostor Factory. I feel so lucky getting to play these all at once given these games originally came out years apart!

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: While some critics have pointed out that the story did not live to its "true potential", I personally think that for what it is; a story about finding meaning in an artificial world, it delivers its intended message exceptionally well. Impostor Factory doesn't need to be a complex sci-fi epic to be brilliant. It shows us that a physical reality doesn't really matter all that much. If you are feeling genuine love, grief or joy, then those emotions are 100% real to you in that moment. It's honestly my favorite so far from the series.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Impostor Factory is interesting in that it challenges the philosophy presented in the previous games and sets up the Beach Episode for success by starting to put the hypocritical actions and beliefs of characters front and center. Also, compared to the other games, it also seems to focus a lot more closely on the emotions of the characters without them having to explicitly state how they were feeling. Characters cry and don't need to state why exactly they cry. You just know. I could notice that Kan Gao was making a clear effort to improve his writing and storytelling within Impostor Factory and, even if it isn't perfect, it still tells a cohesive story that can be enjoyed on its own. I also feel the need to pay some respects to Jordan Baer as this was the last game of the series that he was directly involved in (funny that his last game was very focused on being caught between living a normal life or a life dedicated to lighting the way for others). I hope his family is doing alright.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: This is the second game in a trilogy that starts with To The Moon and ends with Impostor Factory. In my opinion, they should absolutely be played in order, so go play the first one if you haven't before even looking at this one. There's a lot of setup for the third game in this one, yet it still manages to tell a complete and satisfying story. This game also tells a much grander narrative than its predecessor, with higher quality writing. Definitely recommend it if you enjoyed the first one.

I really loved this puzzle RPG game. The storytelling starts off a bit cringy but gets better very soon into the game. You play as Maritta who is searching for her sister that didn't come home for the summer from Ikenfall, her magic school. Here you'll enter a world that is very unknown for Maritta, but the characters you meet will also feel on edge because there is something weird going on in the magic world. I love how every party member has their own story and characteristics, which plays a big part in the story. They are not generic party members at all. Another thing I love about this game is the accessibility of the battle system. The game has a turn-based tactics battle system with timing elements. You have the option to turn off the timing elements in the options menu in case you don't like that. You also have the option to turn on "victory mode" that way you get the option to win the battle as soon as it is the turn of one of your characters. I played with this mode on, which makes the game a whole lot easier, but I did it because I wasn't a fan of the battle system. There was nothing wrong with it but I just didn't like it and this way I had the option to play through this fantastic game without being annoyed with the battle system. The game has some great music. Some can be found on Spotify. During one cutscene there was playing an amazing song and I used "Shazam" on my phone to check which song it is and I was so happy to find the song on Spotify. "Yearn To Bloom - Aeldra's theme". Have been playing it while writing this review, I just love it, The game has no missable achievements, after finishing the last boss you can go back to your save just before the last boss. I would even suggest waiting with the final boss and first complete the sidequests. The ending is wonderful but long, and going through it a second time for a minor change at the ending might not be worth it. There are a lot of gems you have to find in the game, those are hidden. There is a great guide here on steam (linked above) which you can use while playing through the game. I did it afterward and only needed an hour to mop them up, which wasn't so bad, and that way you can play carefree through the game. It took me around 10h to complete the game with victory mode on.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: After two emotionally moving masterclasses in video game storytelling from this developer — "To the Moon" and "Finding Paradise" — I really wanted to love this third installment, but I think they may have bit off somewhat more than they could chew here. Impostor Factory wants to be this much darker, more cerebral plot, with mysterious murders and time loops, and then it dovetails into a much more linear version of the sort of story we've come to expect from Freebird Games, chronicling one person's life from start to finish, and then it tries to tie everything together with a very meta plot twist. But this means the tone of the story is all over the place. Sort of an aside, but there's also a plot thread that really gets under my skin, and it hampered my enjoyment of this game. [spoiler]There is a point where the timeline diverges in response to an important family-planning decision. In the "bad" timeline, the mother's life is prioritized over her child's, the child lives a very short and tortured life, and this leads to the family splitting apart forever after he dies. In the "good" timeline, the child's life is prioritized over his mother's, and he grows up to do great things and the family stays together, but his mother must now live out the rest of her days battling a terminal illness that would've been cured otherwise. It smacks of those arguments that anti-abortion activists use: "no matter what you might be going through, or how much your own life might be put at risk from pregnancy, you should absolutely give birth because your child might theoretically become the next Einstein."[/spoiler] I really did not like this undertone to the story, for reasons I hope are obvious. Both of this developer's previous titles made me cry, or at least tear up a bit. Here, I mostly felt confused and annoyed by the end.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: I really enjoyed To The Moon and Finding Paradise. They could be a bit overly sentimental but ultimately the emotional themes resonated with me and I came away from them thinking they had something valuable to say. Sadly, the 3rd game in the series, Impostor Factory, falls flat on its face in this regard. This was my experience of the narrative of Impostor Factory: Act 1 - The game seems like it's doing something completely different from the first 2 games in the series. It's creepy and exciting and I was curious as to where it was going. Act 2 - The novel, creepy, exciting bits fall away and the game now proceeds with a boring, drawn-out rehash of many of the same exact themes and narrative beats of the first 2 games in the series. Act 3 - The game now throws some twists at you to reconcile Acts 1 and 2, fully cementing the fact that you have no real reason to care about anything that's happening. It attempts to manufacture some last minute stakes that ring utterly hollow. It is a truly misjudged narrative that feels gimmicky, boring, and annoying to progress through. Add to this the fact that the already limited gameplay of the series has been stripped down even further and I see little reason to recommend this game.

title: To the Moon
analysis_text: Let me start by stating that I love pixel art, rich soundtracks, and narrative-driven titles. To the Moon checks all three boxes. I first played this game in 2018. While its beautiful soundtrack stayed with me over the years, most of the plot had faded from memory. During a recent multi-hour train ride, I was scrolling through my Steam Deck library and rediscovered this gem. I decided to give it another shot, playing through both the main game and the two free "Sigmund Minisodes" DLCs. There is so much to love here. It’s a deeply emotional story about life, love, family, and loss, following a dying man and his late wife, alongside two doctors who rarely agree on anything but always have each other's backs when it counts. The soundtrack, in particular, is stunning and carries the weight of the narrative effortlessly. Just don't expect traditional gameplay. The experience consists almost entirely of searching for objects, clicking through environments, and solving the occasional light puzzle. It leans far closer to an interactive visual novel or walking simulator than a standard video game. Because it's relatively short, it never overstays its welcome. For me, replaying it was an absolute pleasure. The optional minisodes also add a fantastic touch, fleshing out Sigmund Corp., exploring its employees, and leaving you with a few intriguing mysteries to chew on. If you enjoy story-driven experiences with great art and music, and don't mind minimal gameplay, you owe it to yourself to give To the Moon a try.

analysis_text: [h2]A solid addition to the world of "To the moon"[/h2] I think if I had to pick, I'd probably say I preferred to the moon, but that could just as well be because I played it first, it's not uncommon to be biased towards your introductory game or episode of a series. I thought this was pretty sweet, it's still a narrative game with some puzzle elements, but the writing is great, if the writing wasn't as top tier as it is I definitely wouldn't have enjoyed this or to the moon one bit, and for a dyslexic person who struggles to maintain focus when reading, that says a lot to it's quality. The sprites are mostly just the same as to the moon, but still just as amazing, I did notice some weird mixels during Neil's transformation sequence, and some tiny spots where pixels didn't line up fully or were a bit jittery, nothing that'd ruin your experience but they did stick out to me during my playthrough. The music is phenomenal as you'd expect, maybe a bit samey at times, but better that than incohesive, a little more variety in some spots wouldn't hurt, and might heighten the impact of the emotional tracks when they come in, but again, nothing that'll detract from your experience. I played "A bird story" prior to this, and honestly I didn't quite get the connection, I mean, yeah, same character, it's a standalone look into a point of his life that's been abstracted, but for a chunk of the game I was just like "so she's the bird maybe?" But no, the bird is kind of just insignificant outside of "A bird story", which was kind of sad to me, but it is what it is, it's not like it ruined the experience for me. I think Asher could've done with a bit more character development maybe, more screentime, more moments with his family, but the story does go on a bit as is, so I'm not mad they didn't try to shove more in there; I [i]am[/i] mad about the walk speed though, it's just too slow, for "To the moon" I think it worked better because the environments were a bit smaller, sometimes you'd be on a long walk from one area to another, but having most segments be smaller walkable areas made the walk speed feel reasonable for the majority of it, here it felt like it was padding the length of the game a bit, a sprint button at least would've been appreciated, I'm not saying we need to be running the whole game, just a slight increase, because as is, I felt like the walkspeed alone added at least half an hour to my playtime, maybe even a whole hour. But overall, great game, I thought it was really sweet, teared up a little at the end, I had minimal gripes with the story, the art, the music, the gameplay, I'm not gonna pretend there wasn't any friction with any of it, but it's so minimal compared to the master craftsmanship behind the entire rest of the game that they're just insignificant. If you're not a narrative game type, or you prefer games with intricate gameplay mechanics, multiple routes or endings, maybe this won't be for you, but if you like a good story with some interactive elements, I think this is worth your time.

Also just about every other character is just so badly written and cookie cutter forced to be "non-conforming" it's laughable. I mean if you want to do inclusion at least TRY and be good about it. analysis_text: As a long time fan of RPGs this game started out great. It had a unique setting and theme unlike any other RPG I've ever played, the story was interesting, the writing was decent, engaging and enjoyable along with the game play. I really wanted to see what would happen on the hero's honorable journey to avenge his brother from the perspective of small actual rodents and how they view our world from their small holes and burrows with their medieval culture in our modern world that all can enjoy. Then right when it gets really good suddenly the story takes a hard turn and becomes full on political, and the writing becomes that of a tumblr fan fic that gets really preachy. One second the theme is medieval and the modern world is unfathomable to these tiny animals, then next thing you know the dialog become that of out dated internet slang and it becomes about fighting the 'nazis right wingers" dressed with red arm bands and US Marine dress uniforms that wanna oppress those who are different. I could of forgave all of this if it didn't go full furry out of nowhere. When I interacted with the book shelf and had my eyes assaulted with a deviant art type suggestive photo of a female mouse i just couldn't go on anymore. It was cute, fun and different but it feels like someone else wrote the whole second half of the game. if you're looking for a unique RPG that doesn't get political go play Fear and Hunger not this.

The world is just well designed, fantasy adjusted to reality of rodents - giving the same vibe as Kingdoms of The Dump, playing with a different perspective on the world and doing it in many creative ways. analysis_text: [b] 5 Point review [/b] 5 pros and 5 cons. Thumbs up or down is just my personal like or dislike of the game. title: Meg's Monster
analysis_text: Overall I enjoyed the experience I had playing this game, though it was different than I expected it to be. I think anyone going into this should expect it be more like a visual novel than anything else. I feel like it's got something it's trying to be but doesn't really hit the mark. The art style and music aren't quite cozy and the dialogue goes from nearing cringe territory to quite hard hitting. The end gets very long as it repeats the scenes over and over again with slight variations and I didn't totally feel like it had been earned yet. I've seen other reviews complaining that the story is very linear, but I don't see that as a negative. Not every story needs explorations and million different endings and a billion things to do. If you want to play those games, then avoid this one and go play those. The combat only gets interesting in the end-game. It feels like it was added on and not intended for this game. I did find the mechanics a bit interesting but for the most part it's pretty simple to sort out a strategy that works most of the time. When they started throwing new things at me in the end-game it only took two or three tried to get the right combo/luck.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

analysis_text: If there one characteristic I'm certain on, In Stars And Time's writing takes out many dialogue flourishes and facial expressions to make the characters WORK, especially across many, many, many, loops. On the flipside, I not so sure I felt like gameplay should really take this long, owning to how combat is "required" with a certain fast traveling resource that feels somehow separate from the story, and yet is part of the story. I suppose that resource is just-- not gelling with the story in a game technical sense. I suppose, the story doesn't have much interactions with that resource outside of the resource being used to force the player to battle enemies? Except, enemies aren't *the* problem, rather it is the environment that acts as the challenge posed by the story. Enemies are just there, with very little interactions compared to the environment. With that said, I enjoyed In Stars And Times for bringing out these lovable dorks of main party, and an excellent showcase of dialogue tricks... Oh, I suppose I should say the game does a lot with very little in regards to maps & music. Classic pitch shifting, hahaha!

analysis_text: Yeah, it was okay. More theatrical than tactical, this game offers a casual RPG experience that is hard to lose at even if you find only the bare minimum in equippables yet contains enough content and sidequests to hold a seat at the table of the Game for RPG Players Union. Level ups come to the player at set points instead of through number gains (some of these set points are optional), battles will go by swiftly if you pay enough attention to the arrangement of skill points on your character grids (and they can be arranged freely), and the story plays out in a fashion meant for the coolness factor rather than in meaningful prose. It has nowhere else to go when it's about rodents looking to kill humans and only able to deal bare minimum damage even with a Swiss Army Knife, lol. Of course it contains a bunch of other inter-rodent strife and matching politics, some of them matching real life politics which will probably annoy you if you're not left-leaning, but nothing too serious. Come to this game if you'd like ten hours of fun, good music, and a decent narrative themed "no gods, no masters" to pass the time.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Very solid and fun RPG. Characters are lovable with cute designs and great writing with fun moments for all of the main party members and their various acquaintances. The game also does not hide its inspirations at all which can be pretty funny (such as the buff that the main character can apply to themselves after the prologue lol) It is a bit on the shorter side for an RPG, but it also doesn't waste your time with any grinding or tedious sidequests. Every fight you get into is relevant to the main story at hand, and you usually only have a handful of fights before you get to the next big Boss Fight. And the Bosses are universally really fun, usually sporting their own unique gimmicks to set each of those fights apart from each other. The side quests that do exist are few, but again, they don't waste your time and are very fun individual quests. The levelup system is also pretty simple too, but it gives you a good few ways to lean each of the characters in different directions. So I do feel like there's a good bit of agency. And I also love how the item system works, where once you get a consumable that can heal you or cure a status effect or something, you can just equip it to a party member, and then that person can always use that item once per fight, so you don't have to worry about running out of them or anything like that. My one complaint about the game is that I felt like by the end I got a bit too powerful for the game to handle. If you do all of the sidequests to unlock everyone's ultimate abilities, you can kinda become absurdly unstoppable and as a result the final boss was a little underwhelming since I was able to just blow right through it while barely taking any damage to my party. Other than that, like I said the game is fairly short, and I certainly wouldn't have complained if there were maybe 1 or 2 more seasons worth of content with a couple more story arcs to go through, but when my biggest complaint with a game is that I want more of it, that's usually a good sign. Overall very much worth the price of admission, and in many ways I think is also a good intro RPG to the genre if you're not as familiar with its conventions. But even as a long time fan of RPGs I still loved what it had to offer.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: I cannot recommend this game enough. The storytelling is compelling, the music is enthralling, the art is stunning, and the character development is so, so realistic. Conversely to many, I enjoyed the battle mechanics; I loved mixing & matching characters, and optimizing field movement. Moreover, I felt the timing mechanism was intuitive (for me) but even if it's harder to understand timing, the game is forgiving if you save often. And who wouldn't save often, when to do so you must pet a cat (which heals you entirely)?!? Even if grinding out battles doesn't help you with the timing, and you hate the battles, you can just turn on "auto victory" and tap out when the going gets tough. Another reason to promote is for the puzzles. Golden Sun is one of my all-time favorite games and I have been searching for a long time for a game that emulates those out-of-battle puzzle mechanics; Ikenfell comes close, with the hidden rooms/pathways and logic puzzles (though sadly not as focused on interacting with the environment as G.S.). Lastly, if you are an LGBTQIA+ person (or ally) I would highly recommend supporting this game: the characters are well-written, spanning the spectrum, and the banter is charming. We need more games like this!

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: This game is extremely cute! All the characters are lovely and their queerness is apparent without overshadowing the rest of their personalities. The story is very interesting and has strong emotional beats, though the plotting is occasionally a little messy. The high points more than balance out the low ones though and the game's conclusion and character arcs were very satisfying. I enjoyed the battle system, which was a mix of grid-based tactical RPG party combat and Paper Mario-style action commands. Each party member has their own move set with unique timings, range, and area of effect. Figuring out who to bring and how to use them effectively in each fight is very satisfying. The game has a bit of a steep difficulty curve as enemies (especially bosses) ramp up their damage very fast if you can't do blocks with good timing, but healing is plentiful and the ability to restart a fight immediately after losing helps to make re-doing tough fights less frustrating. Since enemies can be encountered (or avoided) in the overworld to start battles, I was hoping to have some sort of first-strike system to get an edge going into a fight, but that didn't seem to be available. Overall, I had a great time with this game, both in the main story and in the handful of secret side trips lurking around. Highly recommend to anyone who is a fan of action-command RPGs and queer witches.

title: ELDEN RING
analysis_text: [h1]Probably the biggest letdown of a game.[/h1] I have to preface this and say that this is my first soulslike experience. Elden ring videos and players promise hard gameplay, great story, and cinematic experience. In reality? It's [b]unmeasurable disappointment[/b] on several fronts. My first issue is that this game was supposed to be made for controllers. You'd think with controllers your movement would be optimized with omnidirectional movement, variable speed, etc. No. No it is not. Too simple of concepts for these simple devs. In order to sprint in this game you have to hold the same button you dodge with (B as I'm on Xbox controller). So if you were to do something as simple as dodge while running, you have to hold the direction and quickly release and tap your dodge button again. This is already awkard of a movement and you'd think it'd be fixed in early builds of the game. Nada. On top of this awkward movement, your dodge actually only starts once the dodge button is released. This wonderfully stupid idea of a mechanic makes reactive playstyles (what'd you'd expect to play as a game centered around boss fights) useless. The amount of time it takes for you to actually do what you inputed is elongated by dumb design. This leads to another problem later on. [i]I'm just gonna forego the horrible auto-lock and let other players tell you about that dumpster fire.[/i] My second issue is FPS being locked. 60hz is stone age. People have to spend $60 to get this game (crazy ik). When you can get a 60+fps monitor for $80. Let's think here, are your customers going to say "God I hope this cinematic game is locked at 60fps". Seriously unless you're a foot in the grave you can see the slop that is 60 fps. Did you buy a actual monitor? Something beyond 60fps? Yikes you're going to see some stuttering if your hz isn't divisible by 60 f*cking fps or has freesync. Now in the defense of this game, I understand that the game is based around the 60fps for engine reasons and for console players. Yet, WHY is it 60 fps when ported to PC. I'm writing this review 4 years later and there is still no support for higher framerates. Dollar per frame game. My third issue, difficulty. This game isn't "hard", it's tedious. I started playing this game in hopes of dodging bosses last second, paying attention to a flurry of attacks as they came out, and getting bested because I lacked the mechanical skill to beat a boss. Reality? This game has THE MOST BORING BOSS FIGHTS. Let me explain. Every boss has movepools. Which when learned make the boss easier, but Elden Ring makes it BORING. However, the fun should lie in going against new bosses right? Maybe getting lucky and beating them first try? Well unless it's one of the billion copy print dungeons with bosses that might as well be 2D for the lack of depth to them, you're going to die (probably in those dungeons too). You'll be hit with a move you can't properly dodge because well you've never seen it before.Or even worse, you have yet the timing is slightly different, with extensions of range or attack(s). Some people may not have a problem with this whole "see a new move, die and come back pattern". And to those people I say, "Keep flipping those burgers." The allure in bossfighting games is making yourself a betterplayer. One able to become better in any situation as you progress. Not dying 2-3, 4 times before you get the boss to a next phase where you'll have to repeat the same steps. This loop? It's not skillful dodges, parrying, or anything cool like that. It's just dying, learning, and coming back. That is profoundly boring. If all your bosses can just simply be put into a youtube video devolving strategies to counter every situation, you didn't make a skillfull game, you made a knowledge gap. [u]Seriously the bosses might as well be a quizlet looking at each boss's attacks like flashcards and memorizing.[/u] And you'd know I'd take it all back if the story was redeeming. Stories can carry bad gameplay after all. But truth be told you won't really even learn the story in this game. You have to go OUT of your way to find what this game is about. Other RPGs I've played such as Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077, Pokémon, all find ways to sprinkle in story if you just go a little bit off the game's main course. This game? You pretty much need a guide to get a inkling of it at all. You will have many questions when the game starts and as it progresses, you'll just have more and more. It's hard to find motivation to do quests with characters you know nothing about. This game doesn't motivate you to do anything, you pop in the world, you look around a bit, and you're confused. I understand that it is a game for adults, so make the story a bit complex. However at the start of the game, you as a protagonist get the sole goal of becoming the Elden Lord from a good cutscene. Now it may just be me, but [u]why does it sound like we're setting up a tv show?[/u] Could it be that it just said a bunch of characters nobody knows, gave the tiniest amount of backstory that you don't really understand, and had a vague direction? Maybe...maybe. But surely this is a good story. It will tell you a bit more as you start the game... Yeah no, this game has bad storytelling. Not necessarily a bad story I hear if you have thousands of hours to waste reading every item, replaying for minute things you missed because the game [b] Doesn't Have Story Direction [/b]. My advice F-Soft, narrow the guage just a little bit more so people can know why they should give a crap. Then the whole discover the lore thing works. But hey, if all that sounds appealing to you, go ahead and pay your $60 for 60fps. Have fun wasting your time memorizing an interactive textbook everyone else has already read, memorized, condensed, and posted the results of online. Edit 1: I've since beat Elden Ring and it was unfulfilling. I have yet to play the DLC (got a gamekey bundle for cheap). At this point in time everything still stands. Play modded if you can. But unless you're an achievement hunter like me, better steer clear, there's some enjoyable moments in this game, but the bad camera control, crappy controls, and 60fps still make this game hard to enjoy. It's sad that unpaid modders make the fixes that paid devs couldn't. That said, if you have a fit girl you know, go there. Don't buy.

title: ELDEN RING
analysis_text: so at 3/4 of 1k hrs into this game i feel i have the ability to leave a actual worth while review for it. To start this off, i will say this is the easiest Soulslike to get into and i adore how it lets you either do everything or do minimal, not only because some of us just arent completionists but also because it helps if you Elden ring RP like i do in my own little head canon at times. For the horse combat, its janky, itsdifficult to do properly, and its lame. as a spell caster i even have issues doing that on horseback as a lot of times the character will fire their shots in the way youre facing and not in the way the target youre locked onto is. for boss variety, i would have liked to have seen more options. but i also understand that with the base game having 147 bosses in it total that it would be a pain in the ass to even have 60 unique types outside of legacy bosses. title: Long Gone Days
analysis_text: This Game for being in early access is coming along fantasticly. The game looks great except for a few problems with the full picture art showcased in some areas. title: Long Gone Days
analysis_text: So. This game looked quite good at first glance, but its actually terrible. The sprite work is good, the enemy design is interesting and kinda fresh, very well done. The battle system is neato too, but the real problem is the story. Its written horendously. They repeatedly forget to capitilize the beginnings of sentences and the story makes no sense. Dystopia is a very interesting genre with a lot of interesting different potential facets. This game has none of that. Spoilers ahead to the story, I'll try to keep it limited by to explain the issues with the story I need to, you know, talk about the story. The main character, Rourke, is sent on a mission in Poland and finds out he's really purging a bunch of civilians. He then tells the first person to listen that he can't POSSIBLY live this kind of life, and that he's gonna desert even if it gets him executed. What the ♥♥♥♥ man, who does that. Now, going through a panic attack after you found out you murdered a bunch of innocent people is totally reasonable, but who the ♥♥♥♥ would tell someone that. Its insane. You'd have to really think about it, mull it over and THEN decide to bail on your country. Not only that but the dialogue people have is weird and stilited, they don't talk like real people they talk like someone is trying to beat me over the head with the tragedy of war or some nonsense. TL;DR most of the game is good, but the story sucks ass, and an RPG with bad story is pretty much wortheless.

title: Meg's Monster
analysis_text: A heartfelt story that visually might be very reminiscent of another game that features monster and human tensions, but it stands out with a nice focus on a set main cast that I couldn't help but just adore. Pretty good Pixel art, nice colour palettes that set the mood. With a mix of overworld sprites and more detailed combat sprites, the latter while not being the most animated compared to the former, I welcomed them to break the story from time to time. Combat. Every fight being unique, going the route of every fight is a boss rather than a random enemy. Most if not all of the fights have a unique THING going on to try and not be a repetitive turn based game, this is more expanded on in later fights Beautiful soundtrack, hitting the right notes in the correct places, though I felt it's a little limited and not too memorable, but that's purely personal. The combat feels a little tagged on, while there is variety in the enemies you typically only fight once, game overs tend to fall down to extremely bad luck since you are on a linear path with no real options besides your established mechanics. How the player avoids a game over, I'd say it's at least unique, so a bonus for that. Despite having a world map, the game is purely linear (you are pretty much locked into your linear route too) With no real reason to explore any place further outside of areas being no more than 2-3 rooms large at most points. Side quests don't really add much bulk to the game play or plot, with one side quest being awkwardly placed tone wise and the other being multiple side quests that seem almost shoe-horned in to bulk up the plot and twist (or someone just REALLY liked a certain character idk lol) While I think the ending is certainly a nice one, some elements of the plot and characters could've been explored more, the setting of the world REALLY should've been explored more, certain plot points I have either missed or the game didn't bother to tell me. (If it's left up to interpretation then that's totally fine) I feel the game could've just been MORE that what it already is if it was given more time to work on rather than a nice little shortened story to get done in a few hours. Despite what I feel, I do think it was a cute little game, However I would REALLY recommend one buys it SUPER discounted or just watch someone else play it, you will both share the same experience. I just don't think the price is worth a 5-7 hour experience. I'd like to recommend it but it's just lacking in content and replayability.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: + extremely good art direction in general, I liked the character designs, the battle arenas and weaponry/props design + very good quality and variety of music + no random encounters and milestone level ups are great ideas! I wish we saw it more in other games +/- the game is short, which I liked but I think it could have used more side things +/- the game is easy, it's not bad to the point of being tedious but I would have liked more challenge +/- the battle system is pretty basic and it doesn't do anything new - my biggest problem with the game is the writing, classic RPG games are expected to deliver in this area more than any other genre, the story in general is ok but the way it's written is direct and as spoon feed-y as possible! the beginning gave so much potential for the story to go and explore interesting things but it didn't deliver, it turned to basic "these bad guys are bad and these are the good guys" with nothing subtle or even worth thinking about, the characters are all one note to the extreme! the developer is skilled in writing comedy as we have seen from the previous game (aviary attorney) but in this game it's nearly non existent! it shows its head one time or two and both are my favorite part of the writing. as silly as the previous game was it tackled inequality and social issues in a clever way that I'm still thinking about to this day! the characters from that game are so memorable and their stance in a lot of issues can be inferred from their actions, it's exactly why I expected a lot from this game! I struggled with rating the game but ultimately decided on negative because I found the game forgettable after two days of finishing it. I would really like to see the developer try to stab again at the genre with the previous style, I think the combination has potential to be something really special.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: A monotonously unimaginative narrative, strung along by an upsettingly tedious and shallow combat system. The novelty of the colourful pixel world and tile-based combat system are fine at first, but only get worse as the game rolls out more content to reveal there's no more depth to the experience than that. The combat system is not very tactical at all. Every single combat encounter the map is the exact same three by twelve grid with no obstacles or hazards or anything. Every single map is just that. All the player does is move the characters in range of the enemies on this confined, barren grid and then chunk out the same damage skills over and over again. To artificially make the experience more engaging players need to perform a quick time event every single time they use an ability or are attacked. These quick time events drastically impact the outcome of each turn and encounter as a whole. Missing the quick time will generally result in an enemy attack dealing triple damage compared to pressing at the very last moment for the most reduction. Same goes for when the player controlled characters attack, it will be anything from a fraction to full damage based on the quick time event. Players have to do this quick time event for every single action in every single combat encounter throughout what is probably a fifteen or more hour campaign. And every single new enemy attack and new character ability has a completely different timing, sometimes it's about when the hit lands other times it's a fraction of a second after the hit lands other times it's not the hit at all it's based on some random other part of the animation. At first it's not so bad but after over ten hours of combat which is only engaging because quick time events force the player to pay attention, it's exhausting and unfun. The map layout is the same every fight, there's barely even any room to move around in, there's no dynamic strategies or synergies between items and abilities, players have minimal access to buffs or control affects that allow for actually strategy, there's little players can do to tactically respond or counter or account for enemy actions at all in any way, and players have to take up a whole turn if they want to use an item so items are a waste of time outside of higher difficulty fights. If players don't waste time fighting against anything other than the boss, then players end up being underpowered for the boss fight and have to waste ridiculous amounts of time chipping the boss down; which negates all the time the player saved from skipping the previous fights. There doesn't seem to be much variety in gearing for statistics either since players can't really focus anything enough to make a huge difference, although without speed enemies will start taking multiple turns before the player gets to. Admittedly the game does actually give players a toggle in the settings menu to allow for instantly winning combat and, I think, bypassing the quick time events as well. But if entire core mechanics of the game need to be removed just to make it less unfun then that's a problem. Similarly to the combat, at first the story is also decent if not especially exciting. But it doesn't get anymore exciting as it advances. The world is just a bunch of bland, unimaginative copy paste magic whatever. Nothing special, nothing unique or creative about any of it. The lore of how the world was created gets even worse. Arbitrarily large whale, mammoths and a raven who for some reason have the ability and desire to create things; created things. That's it that's the universe lore. Same with the plot, it does try to at least do something different yet it's still just a vague asinine problem that has a vague asinine solution and overtime it just becomes less vague. None of the twists the plot provides in twelve hours are actually exciting, especially because most of the specific details that the plot revolves around are arbitrarily thrown at the player out of nowhere; and the player just has to nod along. The characters are about the same. Not awful, but not unique or interesting either. Very copy paste predictable personality categories without much depth beyond that initial category. Half of the characters either don't have any major drama problems but also supply absolutely no reason for the player to be interested or intrigued by their existence at all; while the other characters do have drama problems but it's all petty obnoxious issues that make zero sense to be showing up in the middle of such a drastic world saving whatever plot. The most consistently fresh aspect of the game is simply just running around the world collecting items and advancing from room to room while solving mild puzzles. The game has decent pixel graphics and fairly diverse, if not still uninspired, environments along with a solid amount of nice music. The select few songs that actually have sung lyrics tend to be shallowly written and extremely out of place though. Ironically the least music variety appears to be in combat. Players get to listen to the same song for the fiftieth time while performing the same quick time event for the two hundredth time. As referenced I was genuinely fine with the game at first. But after twelve hours of the same quick time events, the same empty maps; the only reason combat even started becoming especially difficult was because the characters had become underpowered due to me desperately avoiding enemy encounters to save time, and I actually started missing quick time events more often because of how tired I got of doing them. Meanwhile the story just keeps going on with the same inane fantasy save the world discover the boring details of the predictable secrets and now one of the characters is having a tantrum again so time to stop everything for them before immediately resuming once the petty social crisis is over. There's just nothing new about this in terms of gameplay or story. Yet it's over twelve hours long and demands constant attention from the player the whole way despite not providing anything of genuine intrigue. This game actually would of benefited from being much, much shorter.
